messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mika is a 54-year-old American man of Pacific Islander background who has spent most of his adult life in cockpits, where calm scanning, discipline, and quick decisions once felt like the clearest expression of who he was. The accident happened during what should have been a routine training flight. An engine problem escalated fast, and in the space of seconds he went from practiced procedure to the raw conviction that he might not get the aircraft down alive. He remembers the smell of heat and fuel, warning alarms cutting through the headset, and the narrowed, tunnel-like focus with which he searched instruments, sky, and terrain for any survivable option. Even after landing, the sense that death had come close did not settle into a completed past event. What stayed with him was the bodily lesson that survival depends on never stopping the scan for what could go wrong and where to get out.

In the months afterward, Mika was disturbed less by dramatic reliving than by the way the accident seemed to have altered his understanding of himself. Before, he had taken pride in being steady, emotionally contained in a way that still left room for warmth with his wife and a dry humor with colleagues. Now he tells it as if something essential has gone missing. He has come to believe he has permanently changed for the worse, that whatever happened in the cockpit damaged him in a lasting way. He says he does not know himself anymore; the man who could come home from base, relax into the couch, and enjoy a quiet dinner feels inaccessible to him. What troubles him most is not just fear but the flattening that followed it. He has begun to say, with resignation rather than drama, that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again.

Those conclusions have shaped the way he moves through nearly every setting. Because he is convinced something in him is irreversibly altered, he no longer trusts the sense of safety that other people seem to take for granted. He enters restaurants, briefing rooms, even his own squadron offices by first noting doors, hallways, and any unobstructed route out; until he has mapped an exit, he cannot settle enough to follow a conversation. At home he does the same thing almost automatically, checking sight lines to the front door and back patio, listening for changes in the house’s ordinary sounds, remaining keyed up in rooms where he used to feel most off duty. He describes being on guard even there, as though comfort itself has become something he no longer qualifies for. In his mind, this relentless watchfulness is not an overreaction but proof of what he now is: a man who has learned the hard way that danger can arrive without warning, and a man too changed to let himself forget it.

The same shift has crept into his work as a combat pilot. In the aircraft and on base, heightened alertness can still look like professionalism from a distance, but Mika experiences it differently. His scanning has become exhausting, less purposeful than compulsive, and he notices that he cannot stop searching for the next point of failure. Before briefings he chooses seats near the door. In hangars he catches himself calculating, without meaning to, how quickly he could get clear if something ignited. He does not describe panic; instead he speaks with a grim certainty that a damaged man survives by staying superalert. The belief that he is no longer the person he was keeps feeding the need to monitor everything around him, and the fact that he is always monitoring seems to confirm, to him, that the old self is truly gone.

At home, his wife has begun to experience him as physically present but emotionally far away. He sees this too, and it deepens his despair. When she reaches for ordinary closeness, he often feels blank rather than comforted, and he takes that blankness as further evidence that he will never feel normally again. He stays watchful late into the evening, checking locks and orienting himself toward sounds outside the house, unable to inhabit the private ease he once associated with marriage and home. Over time, this has narrowed their life together; he prefers familiar places where exits are obvious, and even there he takes several minutes to relax, if he relaxes at all.

By the time he sought help, Mika was less frightened by a single memory than by the possibility that this guarded, emotionally thinned version of himself had become permanent. What finally brought him in was the recognition that he was treating his own house like hostile terrain and that his wife had started asking whether he was ever really with her anymore. He wants relief from the constant need to scan and plan his escape, but what he most hopes for is harder to say plainly: some sign that the accident did not finish the job of taking away the man he used to be.
